title: Longitude Degree Distance Calculator
description: Estimate east-west distance from longitude degrees and latitude using a cosine scale. Original examples explain grid widths, date-line crossings and limits.
summary_sentence: At 60° latitude, a 1° longitude span gives approximately 55.660 km; at the equator the same angular span gives 111.320 km.
quick_answer: This calculator estimates east-west distance as the absolute longitude difference × 111.32 km × cos(latitude). Enter latitude in degrees, within −90° to +90°. The formula describes a parallel-based angular scale; it is not an ellipsoidal geodesic solver or a road-distance calculation. Large spans and near-polar work need particular care.
steps_intro: Enter the longitude difference and the latitude where you want to evaluate it. Decide whether you mean the smaller wraparound span before entering the difference. The calculator does not infer your intended path from two full coordinate pairs.

use_cases.title: Estimate an angular grid cell’s width

body.t: A one-degree-wide cell becomes narrower on the ground as latitude increases. At 60° latitude this formula gives half the equatorial width because cos(60°) equals 0.5. Use that comparison when explaining why a latitude-longitude raster does not contain equal-sized cells worldwide. The width is only one dimension: cell area needs both dimensions and an appropriate area model. A projected grid measured in metres follows different rules from an angular grid.

use_cases.title: Check the scale of a bounding box

body.t: A five-degree longitude span at 55° latitude gives approximately 319.253 km under this formula. This provides a quick check against a claimed east-west extent, but a broad bounding box may cover many latitudes with different widths. State which latitude you used and why. A midpoint latitude can be a rough reporting convention, not proof that the whole region has one exact width or that its boundary follows a parallel.

An extra decimal place has a different east-west ground spacing at different latitudes. For example, 0.00001° of longitude is approximately 1.113 metres at the equator and 0.557 metres at 60°. This explains why coordinate precision cannot be reduced to a single global metres-per-decimal rule. It still says nothing about the accuracy of the device or survey that produced the original coordinate. Preserve the source’s accuracy statement separately from numeric resolution.

Two longitudes close to opposite sides of the date line can be nearby, despite a large raw numerical difference. If your intended span is the shorter one, calculate that wrapped difference before using the tool. For an actual journey between two points, particularly when latitude also changes, use the full distance calculator instead. A constant-latitude arc and a shortest great-circle path are not generally the same route, even when they share endpoints.

examples.label: Worked example · Same angle, different latitude

body.t: For a 0.1° span at the equator, the estimate is 0.1 × 111.32 = 11.132 km. At 60°, multiply by 0.5 to obtain 5.566 km. Nothing about the angle changed; longitude meridians simply lie closer together at the higher latitude. This comparison is useful for interpreting gridded data, not for claiming that every road across those cells has that length.

examples.label: Worked example · Crossing the date line

body.t: For endpoints at 179.8°E and 179.8°W, the raw difference is 359.6°. The shorter wrapped span is 360° − 359.6° = 0.4°. At the equator that gives 44.528 km using this calculator. Enter 0.4° only if that shorter span is the question you intend to answer; the calculator cannot decide whether you meant a small crossing or the long way around.

popular_table.title: One longitude degree at selected latitudes
popular_table.intro: Values use the same 111.32 × cos(latitude) approximation as the tool.
popular_table.note: For wide spans, this parallel-based scale differs from a shortest-path geodesic. It is not a WGS84 ellipsoidal distance calculation.

faq: Longitude meridians converge toward the poles. The cosine factor adjusts their approximate spacing for the selected latitude. A longitude difference by itself is not enough to specify an east-west distance.
Is the result exact on WGS84?

No. The implementation uses a constant equatorial scale multiplied by cosine. That is useful for quick comparisons, but it is not the complete ellipsoidal formula and should not be advertised as survey-accurate.

Within the valid latitude range, north and south values of the same magnitude have the same cosine and therefore the same estimated width. The calculation does not include regional terrain or a road network.
What happens close to the poles?

The width approaches zero because meridians converge. Longitude becomes a poor standalone way to describe local displacement there. Use a suitable polar projection or geodesic calculation for precise work.
Does it automatically handle the date line?

No. The tool accepts a difference, not two endpoints. You must decide and enter the intended wrapped span. For a simple shorter-span calculation, normalize the raw difference to the range 0°–180° first.
Is a wide span the shortest distance between endpoints?

Usually not away from the equator. This formula follows the scale of a latitude parallel. A shortest surface path may bend toward a pole. Use two complete coordinates in a distance tool for that question.
